A co-operative narrative tabletop RPG

Welcome, Traveller

The distant future. Humanity has crossed the stars and become both less and more. Empires rise, expand and fall, and the living, the dead and the unhallowed all vie for a home among the stars.

Against this rises The Traveller: a questing knight with such animus that all who meet him are swept into his orbit. Rumour says he is from another time, another place. His armour, his speech and his ancient spear mark him a stranger. He is neither fully human nor saint, but enough of both to keep the myth alive.

You play his companions. Join him on his quest, and discover the secrets of the galaxy.

Read the rules Download the rules (PDF) Start playing The story so far

How it plays

The Traveller is a co-operative dungeon and space crawl. Instead of playing against each other, you build a story together, using miniatures and terrain you already own as heroes and adversaries. Combat uses D6s and will feel familiar to tabletop wargamers; narrative actions use D10s and will feel familiar to roleplayers, and the two feed each other. A game runs 5–10 rounds, about 1.5–2 hours.

The Games Master’s job is lighter than in a pure roleplaying game. The Traveller and the enemies can be run by dice tables when there’s no GM to hand, and extra players can join as co-GMs to bring out armies and terrain that never see the table.

Who you play

The Pilgrim

Fanatics and zealots, wielders of the flame. They venerate The Traveller. Close combat and Strength, with a minor miracle or two.

The Adventurer

Veterans and soldiers of fortune: pragmatic, dangerous, and out for themselves. Shooting, Dexterity and hard-won drills.

The Mystic

Witches and seers, feared and carefully revered. They wield the uncanny, but not without risk of madness. Powers and Will.

The Traveller

Your companion, never your puppet. Gallant and capable, but also ancient, unpredictable and dangerous. Each round, the dice decide his mood.

What you need

2–4 players and a Games Master, part-time or full-time. A handful of D6 and D10. Miniatures: 3–5 heroes and 5–15 enemies per adventure. A board about 2 × 2 ft, though it scales up or down. This app, on a phone or tablet at the table.

A game night

  1. Build your party. Generate heroes around The Traveller, or keep the ones from last time with their gear and experience.
  2. Choose a mission. Pick a world on the galaxy map, or let fate decide. You get an objective, a villain, enemies, a hazard and a twist.
  3. Draw the tarot. One card for each hero: a boon if it lands upright, a penalty if it falls inverted.
  4. Play. Track Threat, rounds, wounds and enemies as you go. Spend gold at the Trading Post between missions.
  5. Save the mission. Heroes earn experience, the wounded roll for injuries, and the game joins your chronicle in the Lore tab.

Three principles

The rule of cool

If you want to build it, do it or interact with it, and it’s fun, cool or adds to the story: do it.

Own the story

Players have always driven the narrative in the world of The Traveller. Narrative actions should be encouraged and worked into the story.

You can’t really mess it up

If everyone is having fun telling a cinematic story, that is the only thing that really matters.

The story so far

The distant future. Humanity has crossed the stars. Empires rise, expand and fall, and the living, the dead and the unhallowed all vie for a home among them. Against this rises The Traveller: a questing knight from another time, neither fully human nor saint, but enough of both to keep the myth alive.

For the GM only: the secret past

Of the many lives The Traveller has lived, one was as a Knight of the Order of St Lazarus, born of a crusade to protect the dying. Three moments are known, and none have been told at the table: the Birth of The Traveller, the Fall of Moriah, and the Step into Oblivion.

The Lord of Death has always watched him, and has sent the Herald to follow him: Death’s apotheosis, the end to The Traveller’s beginning. At its heart this is a fight between a demigod and death.

The Herald brings a choice. Suffer: watch those around him wither and die, but travel on unhindered. Sacrifice: give part of himself so his companions gain a little of his resilience.

Others want what he is. The Undying are trying to make an artificial perpetual, deathless flesh melded with the machine, and Faust-X is the key.

Act I: The journey begins

Limping toward the edge of known space with a handful of companions.

  1. Episode 1

    Husk: The Tomb World

    Husk was once Acrynax, a shrine world where pilgrims came to honour a great statue and the relic at its feet. When the Empire’s grip weakened and its enemies moved in, the Empire bombed it with plague from orbit and declared it a tomb.

    It was neither quiet nor empty. The crew were greeted by a tolling bell and the parishioners of the Church of the Undying. The mystic Faust-X, half man and half machine, gave himself up so the others could escape. He had believed The Traveller might be one of the galaxy’s few true perpetuals. The Undying took him, and offered him a pact. A relic was recovered.

    Blood pouring from his ears, Crow watched the death world slowly disappear. “We need to go back.”

    “We all saw what path he chose,” said the priest.

    The TravellerCrowGwyedd the priestFaust-X (lost)

  2. Episode 2

    The Wilds of Brawn

    Without their psychic navigator, the crew limped on at sub-light speed for weeks, low on supplies, morale and parts. In range was an abandoned listening post on a feral world the trader maps called Brawn. “Our way forward is now clear,” said The Traveller. “The gauntlet speaks to me. We head to Brawn.” The Herald was waiting there.

    The Crow’s tale

    Parry, brace, parry, brace, parry, feint, parry… Two beasts came crashing through the jungle, and then a blur of the utmost violence, and nothing.

    The Priest’s tale

    Gwyedd steps through the portal and feels the wound open, each point of the star its own shame. He reeks of failure. He stinks of heresy.

    The Seer’s tale

    The Starborn had come. The Herald appeased. Neoma did witness. Neoma will follow. Neoma will guide.

    The Barbarian

    Kneeling before the Herald, his wounds full of flies, Monos felt something he had never felt before: warmth.

Act II: Death Between the Stars

The first convergence of the story, played as a narrative event day at the Salford Lads and Lasses Club in Manchester on 21 February 2026, for charity.

  1. Episode 3

    The first expedition to the Blasphemous Voyager

    Repalda, the one-armed swordswoman, and Graxxx, the ab-human veteran, followed The Traveller aboard the derelict. They raided the old Black Guard facility on the eastern nacelle. Somebody was listening.

    [Transmission, Delta-class encryption]
    Attention all active operatives. Feeds hacked from the Blasphemous Voyager by in-system tech-cult savants. Boarding party raid on the former Black Guard facility, eastern nacelle. Level 9 psychic disturbance detected. Entity known as The Traveller confirmed in Arc segment. All active personnel proceed immediately for interception.
    [End of message]

  2. Episode 4

    The Cyclix Quadrant

    The Voyager breached from deep space, and rumours of priceless artefacts drew fortune-seekers from across the Cyclix Quadrant, the sweep of worlds some call the Arc, the Angel’s Wing or the Scythe. Its arrival threw the dark paths between the stars into chaos. One more rumour persisted: a giant in ancient armour had appeared alongside it. Coincidence, or the hand of fate?

What comes next.

    Children of a Drowned God

    Aqua Moriana, the Darkest Deep: a sea without end in perpetual night. It was home to the Shrine of Nereus, the old man of the sea, until the cult of Pelagia summoned a leviathan that swallowed the dying star above. Now the Cleansing Wake and the Drowned fight over what remains, while the Augmented and the Watchers in the Dark circle.

Side tales

  1. One-shot

    Holt: The Darkling Woods

    A pure fantasy tale. Vanessa Coracle, last acolyte of the sisterhood of Aquis, Drokki Flint, and Therry Speith, a road captain from Harvest, set out from the White Horse Inn to find Black Ron, missing from the mining camp. They found wyrdstones that changed whoever touched them: Therry into a man-boar, and Vanessa into a fishpond. The last fragment, pulled from a small dragon, turned it back into Black Ron.

Core rules

Download the full rules as a PDF to print or read offline. First-pass freestanding rules. Combat tests use a D6, narrative tests use a D10. Meet or beat the target number.

The core mechanic
TestDieStatsUsed for
Tabletop testD6Quality, DefenceHitting and blocking in combat
Narrative testD10Strength, Dexterity, WillClimbing, persuading, hacking, sensing, casting
Challenge rollD10 vs GM dieAny stat as specialtyNew, ambiguous or contested actions

Modifiers are +1 or −1 and never stack beyond ±2. A natural 1 always fails; a natural 6 on a D6 or 10 on a D10 always succeeds. Only roll when failure would be interesting.

Narrative tests and challenge rolls
ResultOutcome
Beat the target by 3+Strong success: it works, plus a clue, advantage or wild die.
Meet or beatSuccess.
Miss by 1Success at a cost: noise (+1 Threat), a wound, lost gear or a worse position. The player may fail instead.
Miss by 2+Failure. The situation moves on.

Challenge roll. The player names the best-fitting stat. The GM picks a challenge die: D6 for easy, D10 for standard, 2D10 keep highest for very hard. The player rolls a D10, or two D10 keeping the highest if that stat is 4+. Higher wins. On a tie, the player chooses: succeed at a cost, or fail cleanly.

Wild dice

The GM awards wild dice for playing to your drive, great descriptions, giving a villain their moment, accepting a complication, or a strong success. Aim for one or two per player per session.

Spend one per test, before or after rolling: add one die of the test’s type and keep the best, or add it as an extra attack die. Hold up to 3. Unspent dice carry over. You can give one to another hero if it makes narrative sense.

Wounds and Toughness

Wounds are how much harm you take before going down: 5 for a standard hero, 9 for The Traveller. They return between scenes or through powers and kit.

Toughness (4 for a standard hero) refills each scenario. Spend 1 to cancel 1 wound as you take it. Spend 2 for a third action once per round. Spend 2 to reroll a failed narrative test. The Rest action restores D3.

Structure of play and Threat

Exploration mode. No strict turn order. Each hero moves about 6" and tries one test per GM beat. Threat +1 at the end of each beat.

Combat mode. 1) Everyone rolls a D10 for priority; the GM rolls for Threat. 2) Players and GM alternate activating one model at a time; each takes 2 actions. 3) End phase: resolve heroes who are down, fire and story beats. Threat +1.

Threat. At the start of each round or beat the GM rolls a D10. If it’s equal to or under Threat, an event triggers, then Threat drops by 2.

ThreatTypical event
1–3Minions arrive, or a hazard
4–6An elite arrives, or the villain appears to taunt
7+The villain or a horror enters the fight
Actions
ActionEffect
MoveUp to 6". Two Moves is a run.
ShootAttack a visible target in range (D6).
FightAttack an enemy in base contact (D6).
ChargeMove 6" into contact and Fight. Uses both actions.
NarrativeA narrative test or challenge roll (D10).
CastUse one power or drill.
HoldShoot the first enemy to move into sight before your next activation.
RestRestore D3 Toughness. Not in base contact.

Shoot, Fight and Cast can’t be taken twice in one activation. Talking is free. Leaving base contact lets each enemy touching you make one free attack with 1 die.

Combat and weapon traits

Roll one D6 per attack against Quality. The defender rolls one D6 per hit against Defence, adding the weapon’s AP to their target. Each unblocked hit is 1 wound; Toughness cancels wounds one for one. Cover gives +1 Defence against shooting. Long range (over half) is −1 to hit. Each extra enemy in a fight gives the attackers +1 to hit, to +2.

TraitEffect
AP(X)Add X to the target’s Defence number.
Deadly(X)Each unblocked hit causes X wounds.
ArtefactOnce per scenario, overcharge for +1 attack die and +1 AP. On a natural 1 to hit, or after an overcharge, it falters until repaired (Narrative action, Dexterity or Will).
ReliableReroll one missed hit die per attack. Never falters or gets disabled.
Explosive(X)Each hit becomes X hits, shared among the target and models within 3". Not in base contact.
FlameIgnores cover. An unblocked hit sets the target on fire: each End phase roll a D6, 1–2 it goes out, 3–6 take 1 wound. An action puts it out.
Powers and drills

Powers are a Will test (drills use Dexterity). Level 1 casts on your stat, level 2 on stat +1, level 3 on stat +2. On a natural 1 it fails, Threat +1, and the peril applies.

Pilgrim priests. A Pilgrim may take one Cleric power, cast on their own Will.

Going down and injury

At 0 Wounds a hero is down. An ally in contact can revive them with a Narrative action (Will or Dexterity): success stands them with 1 Wound. Still down at the end of the following round? Roll a D6 after the scenario.

D6Lasting injury
1Grievous wound: −1 to one stat until healed in downtime.
2Shaken: start next scenario with half Toughness.
3–5Scarred: describe the scar.
6Touched by fate: start next scenario with a wild die.
Experience and levelling up

At the end of each mission, every hero who took part earns experience (XP):

ForXP
Taking part1
Victory / partial victory+2 / +1
Playing to their drive (the table agrees)+1
Hero of the hour (one per mission, by vote)+1

Heroes reach level 2 at 4 XP, level 3 at 9, level 4 at 15 and level 5 at 22. Each level gives one advance: the next power or drill, +1 Wounds or +1 Toughness (twice each at most), a D10 stat improved by 1 (once each, never better than 3+), Quality or Defence improved by 1 (once each, never better than 4+), or a talent.

Heroes who are down at the end of a mission roll on the injury table. The Traveller never levels up. Instead, as the campaign goes on, he remembers.

Bestiary: cults and factions

Each lesser god has a bright cult (allies, rivals, Pilgrim patrons) and a dark cult (enemies). Use the tier stats under Enemies, swap in the cult’s models, and apply its cult rule. Elites and above carry the cult’s trait.

The Traveller

Roll a D10 at the start of each round. He uses Toughness only as armour.

Enemies

A good fight for 3–4 heroes is about 6 minions, or 3 minions and an elite, plus a boss for the finale. Without a GM, roll a D6 per enemy: 1–2 take cover or hold, 3–5 advance and shoot (or charge if in range), 6 charge the nearest hero.

The Traveller’s tarot

Cards painted by Saul Painter. Before each mission, draw one card for every hero. An upright card brings a boon; an inverted card brings a penalty. What each means depends on the card, the world, and how hard the mission is. A card that speaks to the world or the enemy is stronger.

Mission

The deck

Twelve cards. As fate decides, a card falls inverted 30% of the time on an easy mission, rising to 60% on a deadly one.

The Trading Post

The Wandering Peddler trades with anyone who has coin. Buy gear with the party purse, or roll for loot when a hero finds treasure. Items go into the stash, or straight onto a hero’s sheet on the Party tab.

Party purse
0gold

Stash

Loot table and item rules

When a hero finds treasure (or the Treasure event card comes up), roll a D10: 1–5 common, 6–8 uncommon, 9 rare, 10 a unique relic. Only one of each unique relic exists in the galaxy. If they’re all found, a 10 counts as rare.

Permanent items work all game. Once per scenario items recharge when you start a new scenario. Single use items are gone once used. Selling returns half the price.

Weapons from the Trading Post use the traits in Combat and weapon traits. A hero can carry any amount of gear, but only fight with two weapons in an activation.
